title: Lesson 3: Helping Colleagues Without Neglecting Personal Responsibilities
summary: Support colleagues when it is appropriate, but stay accountable for your own work. Offer realistic help, set respectful boundaries, and seek guidance when duties conflict.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Teamwork, initiative, prioritisation, professional boundaries, accountability and mutual support

sections.title: 1. Introduction: Helping others should not mean abandoning your duties
paragraphs: Imagine a therapist at Zura Spa who has a massage appointment scheduled for 3:00 p.m.
At 2:40 p.m., another therapist approaches her.
"Please, can you help me arrange my treatment room? I'm running behind schedule."
The first therapist wants to be helpful.
She immediately leaves her own preparation and spends twenty minutes helping her colleague.
By the time she returns to her treatment room, her client has arrived.
Her towels are not arranged, her supplies have not been checked, and the room is not ready.
The receptionist begins calling her.
The client is kept waiting.
The therapist explains: "I was only trying to help my colleague."
Her intention was good.
However, the way she offered assistance created another problem.
Now imagine a different response.

The therapist says: "I'd like to help, but I have a 3:00 p.m. appointment and still need to prepare my room. Let me finish my preparation first. If you still need assistance afterward, I'll help where I can."
Alternatively, if her colleague's situation is urgent, she could contact the supervisor to arrange appropriate support.
In this second situation, the employee demonstrates teamwork without abandoning her responsibilities.
Helping a colleague is good teamwork. Neglecting your assigned duties in the process is poor judgment.
At Zura Spa, employees must learn to balance two important responsibilities: being willing to support colleagues, and remaining accountable for their own work.
A strong team needs both.

sections.title: 2. What does helping colleagues mean?
paragraphs: Helping colleagues means providing reasonable assistance, guidance or support to another employee when the situation requires it and when doing so is appropriate.
Helping colleagues is an important part of teamwork because no employee works completely independently.
At Zura Spa, the quality of service depends on cooperation between receptionists, therapists, supervisors and other employees.
However, assistance should be offered responsibly.
Teamwork is not simply doing things for other people. It is working together in a way that helps everyone fulfil their responsibilities.
list: Supporting a colleague who is handling several tasks.
Helping a new employee understand workplace expectations.

sections.title: 3. What does neglecting personal responsibilities mean?
paragraphs: Neglecting personal responsibilities means failing to complete assigned duties properly, on time or to the required standard.
A receptionist is responsible for confirming appointments.
She spends a long period assisting a colleague with a non-urgent task.
As a result, she forgets to confirm several bookings.
Although she was helping someone, she failed to complete an important responsibility.
A good intention does not automatically make an action appropriate.
Employees should consider both the assistance they want to provide and the responsibilities that may be affected.

items.label: 1. It strengthens teamwork
items.body: Employees develop a sense of shared responsibility for the success of the spa.

items.label: 2. It builds trust
items.body: Colleagues become more confident that they can receive reasonable assistance when needed.

items.label: 3. It reduces avoidable delays
items.body: Appropriate support can help resolve operational problems before they affect clients.

items.label: 4. It encourages learning
items.body: Employees can share knowledge and help less experienced colleagues improve.

items.label: 5. It supports service quality
items.body: When assistance is coordinated properly, clients receive more consistent service.

sections.title: 5. The difference between teamwork and doing someone else's job
paragraphs: Some employees believe teamwork means completing any task another employee asks them to do.
This is not always correct.
Teamwork requires cooperation, but employees must also understand their individual responsibilities.
A therapist is unfamiliar with a room-preparation checklist.
A colleague demonstrates the correct procedure.
This is helpful teamwork.
However, if the therapist repeatedly refuses to learn the procedure and expects her colleague to prepare the room every day, the situation has become unhealthy dependency.
Helping someone should support their ability to fulfil responsibilities, not encourage them to avoid those responsibilities.
table: Helping when assistance is genuinely needed
Expecting colleagues to complete routine duties
Assuming someone else will handle everything

sections.title: 6. Your assigned duties remain your responsibility
paragraphs: An employee should not assume that helping someone else automatically excuses incomplete work.
A receptionist is assigned to prepare the following day's appointment schedule.
A colleague asks her to assist with arranging supplies.
She agrees.
However, she does not finish the appointment schedule.
At the end of her shift, she says: "I couldn't finish because I was helping someone."
The explanation may describe what happened, but it does not automatically resolve the incomplete responsibility.
A more responsible approach would have been to assess her workload before agreeing, communicate the competing tasks and seek guidance if necessary.
When a supervisor formally reassigns responsibilities or changes priorities, the employee should follow the updated arrangement.
Ownership means managing the duties actually assigned to you, including any authorised changes.

sections.title: 7. Learn to identify priorities
paragraphs: Not all tasks are equally urgent or important.
Before helping a colleague, consider what needs attention first.
A therapist is preparing for a client arriving in ten minutes.
Another therapist asks for help organising supplies for an appointment scheduled two hours later.
The first therapist should normally complete her immediate preparation before assisting with the later task.
Being helpful does not mean treating every request as more important than your existing responsibilities.

items.label: Urgent and important
items.body: Client safety concerns, imminent appointments, essential service preparation. Act promptly.

items.label: Important but not urgent
items.body: Routine stock checks, training, future appointment preparation. Plan and complete.

items.label: Urgent but lower priority
items.body: A colleague's immediate request that does not outweigh your assigned duties. Coordinate or delegate.

items.label: Neither urgent nor important
items.body: Unnecessary conversations or activities unrelated to work. Avoid distractions.

sections.title: 8. The importance of saying "yes" responsibly
paragraphs: Some employees agree to every request because they want to be seen as cooperative.
They may worry that saying "no" will make colleagues think they are selfish.
However, agreeing to something you cannot realistically complete may create disappointment and operational problems.
A colleague asks: "Can you help me organise the supply cabinet?"
The employee responds: "Yes, I'll do it now."
But she has an appointment in fifteen minutes.
She begins helping and leaves both tasks incomplete.
Better response: "I can help after I've prepared for my next appointment. Would that still be useful?"
This response is cooperative and realistic.
A responsible "yes" is better than an unrealistic promise.

sections.title: 9. Saying "no" does not automatically mean refusing teamwork
paragraphs: Employees should understand that setting appropriate boundaries is part of professionalism.
A therapist is attending to a client.
Another employee asks her to leave the session to assist with a non-urgent task.
The therapist should not abandon the client.
She can explain that she is unavailable and direct the colleague to another appropriate source of assistance.
A respectful refusal should not involve insults or unnecessary hostility.
list: "I'd like to help, but I need to finish my assigned task first."
"I can assist after my next appointment."
"I'm currently occupied with a client. Please contact the supervisor if it's urgent."
"I don't have enough time to complete both tasks properly."
"Can we agree on which task should take priority?"
"I can show you how to do it, but I can't take over the entire responsibility right now."

sections.title: 10. Recognising genuine emergencies
paragraphs: Some situations require immediate assistance even when employees are busy.
An urgent safety concern is different from a colleague's ordinary request for convenience.
Employees should not use routine task priorities as an excuse to ignore genuine emergencies.
Client and employee safety must take priority over non-essential activities.
In such situations, employees should follow the appropriate emergency procedure, obtain help and prioritise safety.
list: A client experiences a sudden medical emergency.
A treatment room presents an immediate safety hazard.
An employee identifies a serious risk to a client.
A colleague requires urgent assistance to prevent harm.

sections.title: 11. Helping without taking over
paragraphs: Sometimes the best way to help a colleague is to provide guidance rather than complete the entire task.
A new receptionist is struggling to understand the appointment-booking process.
An experienced receptionist could take over all the bookings.
However, this may prevent the new employee from learning.
A better approach is to explain the process, demonstrate an example and supervise the new employee as she practises.
The goal of helping is not always to do the work for someone. Sometimes it is to help them become capable of doing it themselves.

sections.title: 12. Avoiding unhealthy dependence on colleagues
paragraphs: Some employees repeatedly ask for help with tasks they can reasonably complete themselves.
A therapist repeatedly asks colleagues to arrange her supplies, even when she has sufficient time to do it herself.
Other therapists begin feeling frustrated.
A colleague may say: "I can show you the quickest way to organise the supplies, but you'll need to complete your own preparation so we can all stay on schedule."
If the behaviour continues, the concern may need supervisory attention.
Support should not become a permanent replacement for personal responsibility.
list: Becoming accustomed to others doing the work.

sections.title: 13. Helping colleagues during busy periods
paragraphs: Busy periods are when teamwork becomes especially important.
Reception is handling several incoming calls while two clients arrive.
A therapist who has completed her assigned preparation may offer appropriate assistance, such as helping direct a waiting client or notifying the receptionist about room readiness.
However, she should not independently perform payment transactions or access confidential booking information unless authorised.
Effective teamwork requires both willingness to assist and respect for professional boundaries.

sections.title: 14. Helping without compromising client service
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, client experience is a shared priority.
However, employees should not abandon one client's needs to assist with another non-urgent task.
A therapist is providing a massage session.
A colleague sends a message asking for help arranging supplies.
The therapist should not interrupt the client's session unnecessarily to respond.
She should maintain her professional attention to the client and address the request when appropriate.
A receptionist is processing a client's booking.
Another employee asks her to discuss a personal issue.
The receptionist should complete the client-related responsibility before engaging in an unrelated conversation.
Helping colleagues should support service quality, not interfere with it.

sections.title: 15. The difference between cooperation and people-pleasing
paragraphs: People-pleasing occurs when someone repeatedly agrees to requests primarily to avoid disappointing others or to gain approval.
This can become a workplace problem.
An employee accepts several additional tasks even though she knows she cannot complete them.
She becomes overwhelmed.
Her own duties suffer.
She begins feeling resentful toward the colleagues she agreed to help.
Teamwork should be based on responsible cooperation, not fear of disappointing people.

sections.title: Healthy cooperation
paragraphs: An employee considers:
list: Whether she has the necessary skills.

sections.title: 16. What to do when two responsibilities conflict
paragraphs: Sometimes employees face competing demands.
For example, a therapist may be asked to assist with a room preparation while also being responsible for an imminent appointment.
"Supervisor, I have a client arriving in fifteen minutes, but I've also been asked to assist with another room. Which responsibility should I prioritise?"
This demonstrates accountability rather than unwillingness.
Employees should not silently abandon one task because another person requested assistance.
list: Check whether assistance can be delayed.

sections.title: 17. The HELP method
paragraphs: A receptionist is asked to assist with organising supplies while she is preparing the next day's appointment schedule.
She hears: understands that the supplies need arranging.
She evaluates: checks her current deadline and workload.
She limits: offers fifteen minutes of assistance after completing the urgent booking updates.
She protects: ensures the appointment schedule is completed and communicates any outstanding issue.
This is responsible teamwork.

items.label: H — Hear the request
items.body: Understand what your colleague needs and why assistance is necessary.

items.label: E — Evaluate your responsibilities
items.body: Consider your current duties, available time, skills and authority.

items.label: L — Limit assistance appropriately
items.body: Offer the help you can realistically provide without compromising essential responsibilities.

items.label: P — Protect commitments
items.body: Ensure your own duties remain covered, completed or appropriately reassigned.

sections.title: 18. Knowing when to involve a supervisor
paragraphs: A therapist is frequently asked to complete another employee's preparation tasks.
She is beginning to miss her own deadlines.
Rather than arguing with the colleague, she can explain the pattern to the supervisor and request clarification of responsibilities.
Seeking clarification is not refusing teamwork. It is a way of ensuring that teamwork remains organised and fair.
list: An employee is repeatedly expected to cover another person's duties.
An employee is being pressured to neglect client responsibilities.
A task requires authorisation or specialised training.
Repeated requests for help are affecting performance.

sections.title: 19. What supervisors should do
paragraphs: Supervisors play an important role in creating a supportive environment.
An employee who regularly volunteers to help should not automatically become responsible for every unfinished task in the workplace.
Reliable employees also need fair workloads and appropriate support.
list: Encourage employees to assist one another.
Provide training to employees who need additional support.
Address repeated avoidance of assigned duties.

sections.title: 20. Signs of healthy teamwork
paragraphs: Ask yourself: "Am I someone my colleagues can depend on?"
Also ask: "Do I complete my own responsibilities before expecting others to help me?"
Both questions matter.
list: Employees communicate when they need help.
No one routinely abandons their duties to cover avoidable neglect.
Employees respect one another's time and workload.

sections.title: 21. Practical case studies
paragraphs: Use the four case studies below in discussion. Identify the request, the assigned duty, and whether help should be given now, later or after clarification.

sections.title: Case study A: The helpful therapist
paragraphs: A therapist has a client arriving in twenty minutes.
A colleague asks her to assist with arranging another treatment room.
She agrees immediately.
Her own room remains unprepared when her client arrives.
Expected lesson: Helping colleagues should not result in neglecting essential assigned duties.
list: What should she have considered before agreeing?
How could she have responded professionally?
What does this teach about balancing teamwork and accountability?

sections.title: Case study B: The colleague who always needs help
paragraphs: A therapist repeatedly asks colleagues to complete her room preparation.
She has received the necessary training and has enough time to perform the tasks.
Other employees begin feeling frustrated.
Expected lesson: Teamwork should encourage responsibility rather than dependence.
list: Is the assistance still supporting learning?
What responsibility belongs to the therapist?
How can the employee develop greater independence?

sections.title: Case study C: The busy receptionist
paragraphs: A receptionist is managing several client enquiries.
A therapist who has completed her preparation notices that the reception area is busy.
She wants to help.
Expected lesson: Employees should offer assistance within their capacity and professional authority.
list: What appropriate assistance could she offer?
What tasks should she avoid without authorisation?
How can she ensure her own appointments remain covered?
How does this situation demonstrate teamwork?

sections.title: Case study D: The competing instructions
paragraphs: A supervisor asks a therapist to prepare for a client.
Another colleague asks her to help organise supplies immediately.
Both tasks appear important.
Expected lesson: Conflicting responsibilities should be clarified rather than managed through assumptions.
list: What should the therapist do first?
How can she assess the urgency?
Should she silently abandon one task?
What is the best way to communicate the competing demands?

sections.title: 22. Practical group activity: Should you help now, later or escalate?
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees practise balancing teamwork with personal accountability.
Read each scenario and decide whether the employee should help immediately, help later, provide guidance or seek supervisory assistance.
Group reflection: Each participant should identify one way to support colleagues more effectively and one boundary that helps protect assigned responsibilities.
Expected outcome: Employees learn that effective assistance requires judgment, communication and accountability.

items.label: 1. A colleague asks you to arrange supplies, but your client is arriving in ten minutes.
items.body: Help later. Complete essential appointment preparation first, then assist if time remains. If the colleague's need is urgent, ask the supervisor to arrange support.

items.label: 2. A new employee asks you to explain a procedure you understand well, and you have sufficient time.
items.body: Provide guidance now. Explain, demonstrate and allow her to practise rather than completing the entire task for her.

items.label: 3. A colleague identifies an immediate safety hazard affecting a client.
items.body: Help immediately. Follow the emergency procedure, obtain help and prioritise safety over non-essential tasks.

items.label: 4. A colleague repeatedly asks you to complete her routine duties, causing your own work to suffer.
items.body: Seek supervisory assistance. Offer brief guidance, but do not become a permanent replacement for her assigned work.

items.label: 5. You have completed your responsibilities and notice that reception is unusually busy.
items.body: Help now, within your authority. Direct waiting clients or share room-readiness information. Do not access confidential bookings or payments unless authorised.

items.label: 6. A supervisor assigns an urgent task that conflicts with your existing appointment preparation.
items.body: Seek clarification. Follow the authorised priority. Do not silently abandon one duty because of an informal request.

sections.title: 23. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 3 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the best description of healthy teamwork? Completing everyone's duties regardless of your own workload / Supporting colleagues appropriately while remaining accountable for your own responsibilities / Refusing to help colleagues under any circumstances

A therapist has an imminent appointment, and a colleague asks for non-urgent help. What should she normally do? Complete essential appointment preparation before offering help / Immediately abandon her own preparation / Ignore the colleague without responding
What is a good way to help a new employee learn a procedure? Always complete the task for her / Tell her to work it out alone / Explain, demonstrate and allow her to practise
When should an employee seek supervisory guidance? Whenever anyone asks for help / When competing responsibilities cannot be managed appropriately or require reassignment / Only after an argument
What does the HELP method stand for? Hear, Evaluate, Limit and Protect / Hide, Escape, Leave and Pretend / Hurry, Expect, Lose and Panic

sections.title: 24. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what helping colleagues means in a professional workplace.
Describe the difference between healthy teamwork and unhealthy dependence.
Explain why helping a colleague does not automatically excuse neglecting your own duties.
Identify five benefits of supporting colleagues at Zura Spa.
Describe how a therapist can help another therapist without affecting her own appointments.
Explain why saying "no" to a request is not always selfish or disrespectful.
Describe the difference between cooperation and people-pleasing.
Explain how to respond when two important responsibilities conflict.
Identify three situations in which immediate assistance may be necessary.
Describe the HELP method in your own words.
Explain why supervisors should monitor how additional tasks are distributed.
Identify two ways you can become more helpful to colleagues and two ways you can better protect your own responsibilities.

sections.title: 25. Seven-day balanced teamwork challenge
table: Review your assigned responsibilities before accepting additional tasks
Offer appropriate assistance to a colleague who genuinely needs support
Practise setting a respectful boundary when your workload is full
Help a colleague learn a task rather than automatically doing it for them
Support teamwork during a busy period without neglecting client responsibilities
Reflect on how effectively you balanced cooperation and accountability

sections.title: 26. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Helping colleagues is an important part of the Zura Spa team culture.
A strong employee should be willing to support others, share knowledge and cooperate during demanding situations.
However, willingness to help must be balanced with personal accountability.
Employees should not abandon essential duties, make unrealistic commitments or repeatedly compensate for another person's avoidable neglect.
They should understand their priorities, communicate their availability and seek guidance when responsibilities conflict.
Helping others is most valuable when it contributes to the success of the entire team without creating unnecessary problems elsewhere.
Next topic: Avoiding Blame-Shifting.

remember: Being a good team member does not mean saying yes to every request or carrying everybody's responsibilities. It means understanding your own duties, fulfilling them faithfully and being willing to support others whenever it is appropriate. At Zura Spa, we do not want employees who think only about themselves, and we do not want employees who neglect their responsibilities in an attempt to please everyone. We want dependable people who can balance personal accountability with genuine cooperation. When every employee does her part and willingly supports others, the entire team becomes stronger.
